about: Witla, the lost market at the mouth of the Maas, 793 to 836 and what passes there afterwards. Written 6 Oct 2026 from Design/content/dossiers/witla.md and the spine (cast.gerlef; threads black_stones, hungry_years, dorestad_falls). A draft for the user to overwrite. Read the note first.
note: Witla as a market is known from one sentence, written of its burning (Annales Fuldenses 836). Nothing of it has been dug and no person, building, cargo or toll of it is on record. So every site and every person but the count is ours, built from what is real round the river mouth (Dijkstra 2011), and each says so in its source. Where it lay is not known: the game follows Hoek's guess, a tidal creek on the south shore, and names no modern village.

ports.summary: Witla is a strand market in a tidal creek on the south shore of the Maas mouth: perhaps forty houses on the marsh ridge, boats on the mud, the king's toll post where the Maas and Waal roads reach the sea without passing Dorestad. A merchant comes for the pilot who knows the bar, for Frisian cloth, dried fish and peat salt at the price of the place that makes them, and for the wine, pots and quernstones that come down river and wait here for a wind to England. It is the last dry ground before the crossing and the first news after it.
ports.seasons: The sea is open from about Easter to Martinmas, and the strand is busy only in those months; after the winter floods the pilot sounds the bar again, because the channel never comes back where it was. Sheep are shorn before Saint John's day and the cloth comes to the strand at Lammas; fish is dried in the spring winds; in winter the place is cattle, looms and peat smoke, and the marsh goes under at every storm tide, for there are no dykes.

history.text: One Rathadus gives the abbey of Saint Peter at Ghent a farm at Witle, a small place in the Frisian district: a house, grazing for five cows, and four serfs. Witle is probably Witla. (The gift is of the late 7th century; the note of it may be of the early 9th, in a copy of 941.)

Willibrord gives the church 'in the district Marsum, where the Maas goes into the sea', with a sheep pasture, to his abbey of Echternach. He had it from the cleric Heribald. It stands on the north bank, across the water from Witla.
history.source: Dijkstra 2011, p. 282 (Oorkondenboek van Holland en Zeeland I, not opened)

history.text: At Frankfurt the king names the most that may be asked for a measure of grain and orders his new heavy pennies taken in every market.

King Charles writes to Offa about pilgrims, tolls, black stones and the length of cloaks; the merchants of each realm have the other king's protection again. The quernstones that go to England pass this river mouth.
history.source: MGH Epistolae IV no. 100; spine thread black_stones; Dijkstra 2011, p. 54 (the traffic of the mouth goes south and over to England)

history.text: The law of the Frisians is written down at Aachen. It counts the coast from the Sincfal to the Vlie as its western part, where the blood-price of noble, free and half-free runs as four, two and one.
A fleet of the Danes wastes part of Frisia and comes by Utrecht to Dorestad.
The Northmen come to Dorestad a second time.

This year the Northmen burned the town of Antwerp, and likewise Witla, the trading place near the mouth of the river Maas, and took tribute from the Frisians. It is the only time Witla is named as a market.
history.source: Annales Fuldenses 836: 'Nordmanni Andwerpam civitatem incendunt, similiter et Witlam emporium iuxta ostium Mosae fluminis, et a Frisionibus tributum acceperunt.' (The game's chronicle entry 836-witla-antwerp-burned cites the Annals of Saint-Bertin, which do not name it.)

history.text: On 17 June the Northmen take Walcheren and kill its count, Eggihard, and Hemming son of Halfdan. The emperor hurries to Nijmegen, holds an inquiry into the lords charged with the coast watch, and orders ships built.
On Saint Stephen's day the sea covers nearly all Frisia; 2,437 are counted dead. If anything of Witla still stood, this is thought to have ended it.
history.source: Annales Bertiniani 839; Dijkstra 2011, p. 324 (an idea, not a record)

history.text: Lothar gives Walcheren and the places near it to the Dane Harald. Whether the Maas mouth was among them is not said.
Godfrid the Northman is killed; Gerulf is count on this coast. A ring fort is built for the Rhine mouth. None is known on the Maas.
On 25 August at Nijmegen King Otto III makes Count Dirk II's fiefs his own, Masaland between Lier and IJssel among them.
history.source: nl.wikipedia Dirk II van Holland; Dijkstra 2011, p. 303

history.text: On 29 July Count Dirk III beats the emperor's army at Vlaardingen, on the north bank, where he has built a fort and takes a toll the merchants of Tiel call robbery. The ships had stood off into deep water for the ebb, and men drowned trying to reach them.
history.source: Alpert of Metz, through nl.wikipedia Slag bij Vlaardingen (1018); Dijkstra 2011, p. 303

history.text: The emperor Henry III takes Rijnsburg and Vlaardingen from Count Dirk IV.

eras.text: King Charles's years. A working strand: the toll post at the creek mouth, cloth and fish going out, wine and stone coming down, old Gerlef sounding the bar with a pole taller than himself. The first two summers are hungry; until 796 the stones for England lie unsold above the tide line.

The emperor Louis's years. Gerlef is dead and whoever has his marks takes ships over the bar. New pennies with the emperor's name pass on the strand. There is a beacon watch kept by turns, and each year fewer men turn out for it.

The last seasons. Fleets pass the mouth to Dorestad in 834 and 835; boats lie ready to run, stores go inland by the creeks, and the count of Walcheren comes over to count spears. In the summer of 836 Witla burns.

No market. Black posts on the ridge, tribute paid to the Northmen, the count dead on Walcheren. On Saint Stephen's day 838 the sea goes over everything. A ship crossing the bar finds nobody to ask the way.

A river mouth without a market. The Danes hold Walcheren and Dorestad in their years; a few farms stand on the creeks of the south bank with Rhenish pots on their shelves; ships for England pass without stopping.

The land is Masaland and the count's. From about 1018 a fort and a toll stand at Vlaardingen on the north bank, and the ships of Tiel pay there on their way to England. Of Witla there is a name, and a bank where the nets catch.

sites.name: The creek strand
sites.see: A wide tidal creek at low water: grey mud, a dozen round-hulled boats sitting upright on it, ropes run to posts on the bank. Behind, the low ridge with its thatched roofs and smoke; ahead, the open mouth and a white line where the bar breaks. Gulls, wet rope, the slap of mud under a porter's feet, a smell of weed and tar.
sites.source: invented; the landing is a beach in ports_793.json; the creek is Hoek's guess (Dijkstra 2011, p. 324); the tide of about 1.7 m and the double low water are modern figures carried back (Research/water_levels/north_sea_core.md)

sites.name: The pilot's net shed
sites.see: A turf-walled shed on the bank above the boats, its door facing the bar. Nets hang from the rafters; against the wall leans a sounding pole notched in hand-spans and a lead on a coiled line, tallow in its foot. An old man sits in the doorway looking at the water, not at you. It smells of tallow, tarred net and wet wool.
sites.source: invented; the shed is the one in chain_house_rival step 5; the sounding lead and pole are in Design/research_trade_seasons_and_hints.md 4

sites.name: The king's post
sites.see: At the creek mouth an oak post as thick as a man, grey with salt, and a plank hut beside it with a bench and a pair of scales under the eave. A boat lies ready on the mud with two oars shipped. The toll man stands with a bundle of tally sticks at his belt and watches which way a hull turns: up the Maas, or up the Waal.
sites.source: invented. That toll was taken here from ships on the Maas and the Waal, which did not pass Dorestad, is Dijkstra's reading and not a record (2011, p. 324) (?); the tenth is trade_rules.json

sites.name: The strand market
sites.see: Above the tide line, hurdles laid on the sand and goods on them: bolts of cloth in white, grey, red and blue, stacked grey pots with spouts, quernstones in pairs with straw between, a row of wine casks chocked with driftwood. Women sell from the hurdles; men stand about and say what things cost last year. Wet wool, smoke, a broached cask.
sites.source: invented; the goods are those of this coast: Rhenish wine, Badorf and Mayen pots, lava querns, Frisian cloth (Dijkstra 2011, pp. 308-315); the four colours are Notker II.9

sites.name: Wilsuit's ale-house
sites.see: A long low house on the ridge, the door on the lee side, a bush of green rushes tied over it. Inside, a hearth on the floor, smoke in the thatch, benches, a tub of ale with a dipper, a hatch cover laid over two casks for the dice. Skippers waiting on a wind talk prices; somebody is always asleep in the straw.
sites.source: invented; the dice on a hatch with a skipper in from Witla is Design/town_games.md

sites.name: The cross on the ridge
sites.see: On the highest part of the ridge a wooden cross, twice a man's height, wind-bleached, with a flat stone before it for the priest's book. Graves without markers lie in rows to the east. From here you see both shores: the dune spit to the north, and beyond it, on a clear day, the roof of the church across the water.
sites.source: invented. No church of Witla is known; the mother church is the one 'where the Maas goes into the sea', Echternach's from 726/727 (Dijkstra 2011, pp. 281-285). A preaching cross served from it is our guess (?)

sites.name: Saint Peter's farm
sites.see: A long house with its byre under the same roof, on a low rise at the edge of the salt marsh. Five red and dun cows graze among the creeks; sheep further out are grey dots. By the door a loom stands in the light with a half-made cloth on it, the weights knocking in the wind. Dung smoke, sour milk, lanolin.
sites.source: the farm at Witle given to Saint Peter's at Ghent: a house, pasture for five cows, four serfs (Dijkstra 2011, p. 175). The loom and the people are ours

sites.name: The drying racks
sites.see: Rows of pole racks along the shore, split fish hanging in pairs by the tail, stiff as boards, turning in the wind. Two smoke huts leak grey from the eaves. Children with sticks keep the gulls off and do not always win. The smell reaches the bar before the roofs are in sight.
sites.source: sea fish dried, smoked or salted went up river: 7 to 9 parts in a hundred of the fish eaten at Utrecht and Dorestad came from the sea (Dijkstra 2011, pp. 314-315). The racks are ours

sites.name: The salt burners
sites.see: Out on the marsh, a black scar where peat has been cut below the turf, and beside it mounds of grey ash and a clay pan steaming over a low fire. A man and a boy rake the ash and pour sea water through it. The smoke is thick and brown and lies flat along the ground. Everything here is the colour of ash, and so are they.
sites.source: salt was burned from salt-soaked peat in Zeeland; in South Holland only the islands in the Maas mouth were fit for it (Dijkstra 2011, pp. 308-315). That it was made at Witla is our guess (?)

sites.name: The mark on the dune
sites.see: At the seaward end of the ridge a mound of turf with a tall post on it, a cross-piece near the top and a basket of dry furze at its foot. From the mound the whole mouth lies open: brown water, the bar breaking white, the far shore a thin line. A ship coming in puts the post over the end of the ridge and holds it there, in the years when that still works.
sites.source: invented; 'the old mark on the dune is no use now' is the pilot's word in chain_house_rival step 5. Fires on sea-marks: the emperor's at Boulogne, Royal Frankish Annals 811

people.name: Gerlef
people.trait: The pilot of the Maas mouth: knows where the channel went after each winter's floods, and the Thames to the Strand; tells the truth about water and lies about his age.
people.want: A son or a pupil to take the marks from him before his eyes go.
people.fear: Going blind; a new sandbank where his father's channel was.
people.voice: Talks to the water more than to the merchant: 'she shoals here', 'she runs north of the bank now'. Answers a question about himself with a fact about the tide.
people.looks: Nearly fifty and looks older, wiry, white stubble, a salt-stiff hooded cloak, a sounding pole taller than himself and a lead on a line with tallow in its foot.
knows: where the channel over the bar runs this year, and when the ebb will set you on it
the Thames marks as far as the Strand at Lundenwic
the creeks through to the Scheldt and Walichrum
whose ship is expected, because he is paid to be free for it
who came down river on the last wine boat and who went over the water

ties.note: the same person
Thiadbod pays him by the year, so others wait
taught Aldger the Thames marks
his daughter; she tells him what he can no longer see and pretends she is only talking
his daughter's son, eight years old in 793, the only one who asks him the right questions
they have watched the same water for twenty years and agree about nothing else
the reeve at Lundenwic once let his ship lie a tide without the fee, and has not forgotten it
sleeps at her house when he brings a ship up the river, and pays in the state of the channel
says a river pilot need only know left from right; Aldlef says the sea has no banks to hit
rows the priest over for nothing when the ebb is too strong, and is prayed for by name
sleeps by her fire when he works the Scheldt mouth, and pays in news
lodged with her the winter the ice shut the river, and paid in stories
showed the ferryman how to keep marks in his head, the winter he was iced in below the king's house
a cheerful young pilot from the terps who talked at him for a whole night at Dorestad
the Oostergo pilot: they agreed for a whole night at Dorestad that skippers are fools
lay windbound at Gipeswic a week with him once; they compared marks, and each thought the other a liar
brought her husband's boat home without him, and took nothing for it
brings the steersman at Dofras a cheese each time and asks the same question about the sands
trades marks with him, the Maas mouth for the strait; neither gives his best one
sleeps in his loft between tides and pays in news of the sands
drinks one cup at her house, slowly, and tells her how the sands lie
a river pilot far to the south whom he has never met: wine skippers carry each one's greeting, and each one's opinion of the other's river
an island steersman of the salt bay: Frisians in for salt bring his greeting north, and Gerlef sends back the state of the bar
the pilot of the Dee, never met: skippers carry each one's sayings to the other, and each thinks the other must be a sound man

lines.greet: She is making now. You came over the bar on the last of the ebb with a hand's breadth of water under you, and I watched you do it, so do not do it again.
lines.greet_again: So it is you again. She runs north of the bank since the floods, so forget whatever I told you at Easter.
rumour: Thiadbod's big ship is looked for by Lammas, and until she is in I take nobody else over. He pays me for that, though I never said that I liked it.
The English reeve turns Frankish hulls back on the Thames. A Frisian with a gift and a story still lands. I have seen both in one tide.
There is stone under the water off the south head, squared, older than anybody. At a low ebb it breaks the surface. I have put my pole on it.
lines.saying: The bar has no friends, only people it has not met yet.
lines.age: I am forty, and I have seen that bar move nine times in fifty years, so ask me about the water instead.
lines.eyes: The far mark is soft this year, which is the haze, as it was the haze last year too.
lines.friend: Bring the boy a lead line from Lundenwic, the English kind with the hollow foot. Do not say I asked.
lines.farewell: Go out on the first of the ebb and not on the last of it, and keep the post over the end of the ridge until she lifts.

people.source: invented: the spine's cast.gerlef, with the same facts; the line about his age is the chain's (chain_house_rival.s05.pilot_age). The squared stone is what Jan Kluit of Brielle saw at a very low tide in 1752 (Dijkstra 2011, p. 454)

people.name: Gerbrand
people.trait: Gerlef's grandson: quick, sure of himself on the water and unsure of himself anywhere else; sounds a channel twice because his grandfather is no longer there to say once was enough.
people.want: To be called the pilot, not the old pilot's boy; and somewhere to take the marks if this strand is lost.
people.fear: That he learned the mouth from a man who could no longer see it, and that some of what he knows is ten years out of date.
people.voice: His grandfather's turns of speech in a younger mouth; says 'she' of the river and 'they' of everybody up it.
people.looks: In 812 about twenty-seven, long-armed, fair hair tied back with a thong, bare feet grey with mud to the knee, the old sounding pole with fresh notches cut between the worn ones.
knows: the bar and the creek, tide by tide
which marks his grandfather sold, taught or kept, and to whom
from 834: where the fleets lay the night before they went up river, and how many keels
who on the strand has a boat ready to run and who has buried something

ties.note: his mother's father; the pole is his and so are the sayings
his mother; she still counts his boats in at dusk
will not be kept by the year as his grandfather was, and Thiadbod's house does not forgive a refusal
from 834 the count has him watch the mouth and light the mark; he is paid in promises
Aldger had the Thames marks from the old man and gave some of them back to the boy

lines.greet: You want to go over the bar, as everybody does, so sit down. The water will tell us when, and it is not telling us yet.
lines.greet_again: I know your boat by how she sits, and my grandfather knew your house, so come along and I will take you over myself.
rumour: They went up by night at Whitsun, with more keels than I have fingers twice over. They asked for no pilot, and that is the part of it I do not like.
The count wants a fire on the mark when I see sails. A fire tells them where the houses are as well as it tells him.
The old channel is filling. My grandfather would say it is the river being a river. I say tell the king's man before a wine ship finds it.
lines.saying: Sound it twice, because the first time is for the river and the second time is for you.
lines.heir: He said your father's house paid in silver and asked about the water first. That was the best he said of anybody.
lines.after: Witla was forty houses and a beach, and now it is only a beach. I still know the bar, and I will work for bread and a place by the fire.
lines.farewell: Go on the first of the ebb, and keep north of where you think she is, because she has moved again.

people.source: invented: the heir the spine asks for ('the pilot's family take their marks elsewhere'); Ger- kept from his grandfather as heirs' names alliterate (npc_text_encounters.md 2.5), -brand as in Liudbrand. His words after the burning are those of the card long.witla.burned_836, where 'forty houses' is the pilot's word and nobody's record (?)

people.name: Wilsuit
people.trait: Gerlef's daughter: brews, lodges skippers waiting on a wind, and keeps in her head what each of them owes and what each of them said when he had drunk.
people.want: Her son to have the pole and not the sea; and her father to stop going out alone at dusk.
people.fear: A dusk when one boat too few comes back into the creek.
people.voice: Brisk and kind in the same breath; asks if you have eaten before she asks if you can pay.
people.looks: About thirty in 793, strong forearms, a linen head-cloth pinned with one bronze pin, a grey gown kilted up out of the wet, a dipper in her hand and a ring of tally sticks on a cord.
knows: who is in the creek, what they carry and how long they have waited
what was paid for cloth, wine and stone on the strand this week
who is hiring and who was paid off, and why
that her father's eyes are worse than he says

ties.note: her father; she reads the far mark aloud for him as if by chance
her son
her malt comes down river on credit from the widow's storehouse at Dorestad
he pays his score once a year, in cloth, and she lets him think it is a secret
feeds the priest when he comes over the water, and is told off for brewing on Sunday
girls on this strand together; she was born free and has never mentioned it

lines.greet: You are wet to the knee and there is nothing in you, so sit by the fire. The ale is new and the bread is yesterday's, and the price is the same for both.
lines.greet_again: I kept your corner for you. A man in from Walichrum wanted it, and I told him that you snore, so sit down.
rumour: They say the toll man up river was changed at Easter, and that the new one counts the casks himself. Ours has not been changed, and ours cannot be surprised by anything.
Three skippers here are waiting on the same wind for Lundenwic, and the first one over will sell dear, though I am only saying what I hear.
Radward swears that there will be no cloth before Lammas, and Radward has a boat full of cloth, so make of that what you like.
lines.saying: Dear is the welcome guest to the Frisian wife. Dearer still when he pays before he sleeps.
lines.father: He sees the bar well enough, but it is the mark behind it that he asks me about. Say nothing of that to him.
lines.sunday: The priest says I may not brew on the Lord's day. I asked him whether the ale knows what day it is.
lines.farewell: Go with God, and come back with whatever you owe, because I have it notched.

people.source: invented: Wil- as in Willibraht, -suit as in Meinsuit (Altfrid I.25). Her saying turns the Exeter gnomic verse on the Frisian wife (Thorpe 1842). Sunday work is fined four shillings in the Frisians' law (Lex Frisionum XVIII)

people.name: Folcrad
people.trait: The king's toll man at the post: slow, exact, impossible to hurry and hard to dislike; takes the tenth and not a penny more, and expects to be thanked for it.
people.want: A quiet year, a full tally at Michaelmas, and a son-in-law who can count.
people.fear: The king's men from up river arriving on the one day his sticks do not agree.
people.voice: Says everything as a sum, in full: so many casks, so many pennies, so many days. Dry as an old cask.
people.looks: About forty-five, broad and slow, a grey short cloak with a plain iron pin, a bundle of notched tally sticks at his belt and a small pair of scales he polishes when he thinks.
knows: what every hull paid here this season, and so what she carried
the king's rule of the day: the new penny, the grain price, who may not land where
the Frisians' law as it is said on this coast: four, two and one
which skippers show a charter and which only say they have one

ties.note: his tally sticks go up river to the count's steward at Michaelmas (?)
the steward checks his weights and he checks the steward's
the pilot tells him what is coming over the bar before it comes
Thiadbod gives every officer a gift; this one weighs it, notes it and sends it up river with the tally
a small old quarrel over a bolt counted twice, kept warm by both for the pleasure of it
the toll man at the fort on the Scheldt; they send each other word of bad payers by any skipper going round

lines.greet: Tell me the hull, her master, where she is from and what is in her, and then pay the tenth. After that we can talk about the weather like Christian men.
lines.greet_again: It is you. You had six casks at Pentecost and paid in good coin, and I notched it. What is it today?
rumour: The king has made the penny heavier, and the old ones go to the mint at Dorestat at a loss. I do not make the loss, I only name it.
No English hull may trade on this shore, by the king's word. Nobody has told me if a Frisian with English cloth is an English hull.
No measure of wheat may be sold above four pennies now, in plenty or in dearth. I have the new measure here, and yours looks small beside it.
lines.saying: They say that Charles was sold a short cloak at the long price, and that he asked what use such napkins were. We kept the silver all the same.
lines.law: For a noble, a free man and a half-free man it is four, two and one. That is how the blood-price runs here, and the oath-helpers with it, so bring your kin or bring silver.
lines.gift: That is a handsome gift. I will weigh it, notch it, and send it to the count with your name. Do you still wish to give it?
lines.farewell: You are paid and notched, so you may go. The river is the king's public way, and you are not to lie across it.

people.source: invented. A toll-taker at the Maas mouth is likely and not proven (Dijkstra 2011, p. 324) (?). Folc- and -rad are both attested Frisian name parts. The cloak joke is Notker I.34 (Grant 1907); the price cap and the new penny are Frankfurt 794; 4:2:1 is Dijkstra 2011, p. 359; the blocked public way is Lex Frisionum, Additio VI

people.name: Radward
people.trait: A skipper of this strand with one round-hulled boat: runs cloth and dried fish to Walichrum and over to Lundenwic, dices for anything, loses calmly and wins loudly.
people.want: To be first over the water after any bad news, when prices are stupid.
people.fear: Thiadbod's big ship, which carries in one crossing what he carries in four.
people.voice: Easy and sly; gives a price by telling a story about somebody else who paid it.
people.looks: About thirty-five, lean, sunburnt, a short blue Frisian cloak thrown back, a leather dice cup at his belt beside his knife, a scar through one eyebrow.
knows: what cloth and fish fetch at Walichrum and on the Strand at Lundenwic, as of his last crossing
which way round the ban is being kept this month
who dices fair on this coast
what Thiadbod's men are buying up, a week before the price moves

ties.note: undersold on every crossing, and says so to anyone
promised the reeve at Lundenwic a gift for a landing during the ban and has not yet brought it
his score at the ale-house is a year long
the bolt counted twice
buys her cloth before it is off the loom, at a price she regrets by Lammas
takes the Mainz man's wine on over the sea to the English

lines.greet: Here is a new hull, so sit down. I have four pennies on the hatch that say you cannot beat a five.
lines.greet_again: You owe me a throw, or else I owe you one. Wilsuit will know which, because she notches everything.
rumour: A man I know landed English cloth at the Strand with a gift for the reeve and a story about pilgrims. I will not say who he was, because he is a modest man.
Thiadbod's men are buying every quernstone on the river. Either he knows something about the English king or he likes stones.
The toll man up river was changed at Easter, and the new one cannot be bought, though I would give him a year.
lines.saying: The first boat sells dear, the second sells, the third carries it home again.
lines.win: I threw six and stood on it, which is not luck but knowing when a thing is good enough.
lines.lose: That is eleven, so I laugh and I pay, and I tell you something worth four pennies, which is not to sell fish at Walichrum this week.
lines.farewell: If you reach the Strand before me, say nothing about cloth. If I reach it first, I never met you.

people.source: invented: the 'Radward, a skipper in from Witla' of Design/town_games.md, with his throws and his news of the changed toll man; the name is in names_placeholder.json

people.name: Bernrad
people.trait: The priest of the church across the water, Saint Willibrord's gift to his abbey: rows over on feast days to say Mass at the cross, bury the dead and count who came.
people.want: A roof over the cross at Witla and a bell to call the strand, so that he need not shout against the wind.
people.fear: The place in the fen behind his own church that people still call the shrine, and how well they know the path to it.
people.voice: Patient, a little hoarse; begins with scripture and ends with cows.
people.looks: Nearly forty, thin, tonsured, a brown wool tunic patched at the elbows, bare muddy legs, a small book in a sealskin bag hung round his neck and an oar over his shoulder.
knows: the feasts and fasts, and which days nobody may work or sail
who is buried at the cross and who still owes for the grave
that the church is Echternach's while the tithe of Maasland is Saint Martin's of Utrecht, and what that quarrel costs
what is still done at night in the fen, though he will only half say it

ties.note: his church answers to the abbot of Echternach, and the bishop's men come for Saint Martin's tithe on the same marsh
says he heard Liudger teach at Utrecht as a boy, and has dined out on it since (?)
she feeds him; he scolds her for brewing on Sunday; neither minds
writes down for her, on a scrap, what her daughter's freedom would cost
the pilot brings him over the water for nothing when the ebb is too strong to row
the priest at the fort on the Scheldt; they share one copy of the feasts and argue about its dates

lines.greet: God keep you. You are in time, because Mass is at the cross when the tide turns, and the tide is the only bell I have.
lines.greet_again: You are the merchant who stood through the whole Mass. There were four of you who did, and I remember all four.
rumour: Alcuin wrote that this land bears neither oil nor wine, and called our bishop mighty in cows. He meant it kindly, or so I think.
The heathen men fell on a holy island in the north, before Saint John's day. A letter went up river about it. I saw the seal, not the words.
There is a place behind my church that the people call the shrine. Nothing stands there now, and they walk to it all the same.
lines.saying: Frisia bears neither oil nor wine. So the lamp burns butter and the feast is porridge, and God sees it as well.
lines.hunger: The poor are on every path this year. A measure of rye at the king's price would be remembered here longer than you think.
lines.bell: All I want is one small bell, and I have priced it. It costs what a skipper loses in one bad crossing and never speaks of.
lines.farewell: Go with God, and keep Sunday, even at sea. The fine is four shillings, and the other cost is more than that.

people.source: invented: no priest of the Maas-mouth church is named. The church and its gift to Echternach, Saint Martin's tithe, and Harg ('heathen shrine') in the fen behind Vlaardingen are Dijkstra 2011, pp. 281-288, 301. Alcuin's poem down the Rhine (Carmina IV) is paraphrased, not quoted. The Sunday fine is Lex Frisionum XVIII

people.name: Thiadlint
people.trait: One of the four serfs of Saint Peter's farm: keeps the five cows and weaves the best cloth on the strand, a bolt of which goes to Ghent each year whether there is bread or not.
people.want: To buy her daughter Liaflint free of the abbey before the girl is old enough to be given with the farm.
people.fear: A murrain among the cows, which would be counted as her fault and her debt.
people.voice: Low and exact; names a price once and then looks at her loom until you answer.
people.looks: A little over thirty, small and straight-backed, hair under a plain grey cloth, a gown of her own good weave with no brooch to it, fingers dyed blue to the first joint, a weaving sword of whalebone in her belt.
knows: cloth: which bolt is honest, which was stretched, and how long a cloak should be
what the farm owes Ghent each year and what is left after
the salt marsh: where sheep drown, where the creeks can be waded
what a half-free woman's price is by the law, and how far she is from having it

ties.note: the farm is Saint Peter's of Ghent; from about 815 its lay abbot is Einhard, who has never seen it (?)
he buys her cloth before it is woven and she is always a bolt behind
the priest wrote her daughter's price on a scrap she keeps in the roof
they were girls on this strand together; one was born free
the abbey's cellarer, who knows her by one bolt of cloth a year and five cows

lines.greet: You may feel it, but do not pull it. That bolt is for Ganda, and these two are mine to sell, at forty-eight pennies.
lines.greet_again: You paid what I asked last time and did not pull the cloth. I have kept one back for you.
rumour: The Franks say our cloaks have grown short. Wool has not grown cheap. Somebody up river is cutting three cloaks from a two-cloak bolt, and it is not me.
The cows gave little this spring, and the abbey's due is the same as ever. There are five cows, four of us and one bolt, and Ganda can count.
Radward says that there will be no cloth before Lammas. There is cloth, and it is Radward who has it.
lines.saying: A cloak of the right length sells itself, but a short one needs a merchant.
lines.daughter: Her price is written on a scrap that I keep in my roof. I cannot read it, but I know the number.
lines.hunger: We ate the seed barley at Candlemas. If you carry grain, sell it here at the king's price and I will weave for you first.
lines.farewell: Go well, and if you pass Ganda, tell the cellarer that the cows are alive, because he will ask about nothing else.

people.source: invented: the farm with grazing for five cows and four serfs is real (Dijkstra 2011, p. 175); its people are not named. Thiad- and -lint (as in Folclint) are attested. The cloaks are Charles's complaint to Offa in 796 and Notker I.34. Einhard as lay abbot of Saint Peter's at Ghent: realms/frisia_lotharingia.json (?)

stories.title: Paid by the year
stories.summary: While the kings quarrel and the ports are shut, the pilot of the Maas mouth is kept by Thiadbod, so every other skipper waits a tide behind Thiadbod's ship, and the quernstones meant for England pile up on the strand. A merchant who asks Gerlef about the water, and not about his price, can be taught what Thiadbod only rents: the marks over the bar and up the Thames to the Strand.
stories.picture: The creek at low water under a flat grey sky: pairs of dark quernstones stacked in straw above the tide line, a big blue-sailed ship coming in over the bar, and an old man with a tall pole walking out to meet her past a row of small boats that are not going anywhere.

beats.text: Gerlef will not take you over: Thiadbod's ship is looked for, and he is paid to be free for her. He says so plainly and looks at the water. You may wait a tide, pay him double to go now, or sit and ask where the channel went this winter.
Quernstones from up the Rhine, cut to the length the English want, lie unsold and cheap: twelve pennies a pair is asked and eight is taken. Radward says Thiadbod's men are buying them all the same.
The reeve Wighelm turns Frankish hulls away, but a Frisian who comes in by the pilot's own marks, with a gift and a story, is let lie a tide. He asks after Gerlef by name.
Thiadbod is friendly about it: of course the old man is his by the year, anybody could have thought of it. He offers to let you follow his ship over the bar, for a share.

The first ship of the summer brings word of the king's letter: the ports are open. Every stone on the strand is sold before the ebb, and Gerlef takes four ships over the bar in one tide, Thiadbod's last.
Radward dices at Wilsuit's while he waits his turn behind Thiadbod's ship, and says what a cask of wine fetches over the water when a Frisian can land it.

endings.how: Came back season after season, asked about the water first, and brought the boy a lead line from Lundenwic.
endings.text: Gerlef walks you along the mark at dead low water and says each thing once. After that you cross the bar and reach the Strand without him, and he pretends not to watch you do it.
endings.reward: The Maas bar and the Thames to the Strand need no pilot for this house (in the engine's words: learn, for the Maas-mouth and Thames marks); Gerlef a fast friend; the reeve at Lundenwic is easier to a man who knows the river.

endings.how: Took Thiadbod's offer and crossed in his wake for a share.
endings.text: You are never aground and never first. Thiadbod's steersman learns your cargo by how deep you sit, and the price at Lundenwic has always just fallen when you land.
endings.reward: Safe crossings at the Maas mouth while Thiadbod lives; a share of each crossing's profit goes to him; Thiadbod easy, Radward cool.

endings.how: Bought the cheap quernstones while the ports were shut and was first over after the letter of 796.
endings.text: The stones nobody wanted at eight pennies sell on the Strand for the first-cargo price. Thiadbod's men, a tide behind, unload beside you and say nothing at all.
endings.reward: One very good cargo (silver, in the range of a good voyage twice over); a price word for quernstones at Lundenwic; Thiadbod's notice, which is not a gift.

stories.reward: The pilot's marks, or a safe wake, or the first cargo after the peace: each a different standing with Gerlef, with Thiadbod and with the reeve at Lundenwic.

stories.title: A pole taller than himself
stories.summary: Gerlef's eyes are going and he will not say so. His daughter's boy is too young, Thiadbod would buy the marks for his own steersman, and a pilot's knowledge dies in a winter if nobody has it by heart. Who holds the pole after 812 decides what the Maas mouth is to this house for a generation.
stories.picture: Dusk on the bank above the creek: an old man in a stiff hooded cloak holding a sounding pole upright, a barefoot boy beside him holding it too, lower down, both looking at the same white line of the bar; a woman in the lit door of the ale-house behind them, counting boats.

beats.text: Wilsuit tells you quietly that her father sees the bar but not the mark behind it, and asks you to say nothing. The boy Gerbrand, eight years old, can already name the creeks in order.
Gerlef asks, sideways, whether a boat like yours has room for a boy as far as Lundenwic and back: one crossing, to see the Thames marks with young eyes while there is someone to check him.
The boy sounds his way up to the Strand with a borrowed lead and is wrong twice. Aldger, who had these marks from the old man, puts him right without saying he was wrong.
Thiadbod's man lets it be known that his master would pay well, to a friend of the old pilot, for the marks written down or said over: forty pennies for an evening's talk.

Gerlef goes out on the flats alone at a spring ebb to find the new channel by feel. Whoever he has taught goes after him with the pole. He comes back on the boy's arm, or on yours, or the tide brings the pole in without him.
On the flats of Westergo a young pilot quotes Gerlef as other men quote the priest, and asks whether the old man can still see the far mark.

endings.how: Carried Gerbrand to Lundenwic and back and kept the old man's secret.
endings.text: In 812 the pole passes to Gerbrand with nothing said. He takes your house's ships over the bar first and for nothing, and tells your heir why.
endings.reward: Free pilotage at the Maas mouth for this house while Gerbrand lives, and a pilot to hire who knows the Thames; the friendship is inherited (npc pilot feeling carried to the heir); Wilsuit keeps a corner for you.

endings.how: Said the marks over to Thiadbod's man for forty pennies.
endings.text: Thiadbod's steersman crosses without a pilot from then on, and Gerlef, who is not told how, stops talking about water when you are in the shed. After 812 the pilot at Witla is Thiadbod's.
endings.reward: Forty pennies and Thiadbod's good word once; after 812 this house waits a tide at the bar and pays double; Gerlef and Wilsuit cool to wary.

endings.how: Did nothing; called seldom; the old man went out alone.
endings.text: The pole comes in on the flood. Gerbrand learns the bar again from nothing, and for three summers ships touch on banks that used to have names.
endings.reward: Nothing gained: from 812 for some years the crossing is doubtful for everyone, your rivals as well; Gerbrand owes you nothing and can still be won.

stories.reward: A pilot who is your friend for two lifetimes, or forty pennies and a closed door, or a dangerous bar for everybody.

stories.title: Five cows for Ghent
stories.summary: In the hungry summers the farm that Rathadus gave to Saint Peter's still owes the abbey its bolt of cloth and its cheeses, and the four serfs on it have eaten the seed barley. A merchant with grain can sell it here at the king's price or the strand's price, and what he does is remembered at the loom, at the cross and at the toll post.
stories.picture: The long house at the marsh edge in thin morning light: five lean cows, a loom by the door with a half-woven grey cloth, a small straight-backed woman measuring grain from a merchant's sack into her own bowl while a toll man with tally sticks looks on from the path.

beats.text: Thiadlint will sell her own two bolts for bread, not silver: there is none to buy. The abbey's bolt she will not touch. A measure of rye is asked at ten pennies on the strand.
Folcrad has the king's new measure and the king's price: wheat at four pennies and no more, rye at three. He checks your measure against his and says nothing about what was charged last week, once.
Bernrad asks from the cross, by name, for whoever sold bread cheap. If it was you, the strand knows it by the next tide.
The cellarer of Saint Peter's takes the Witle due from your boat, counts the cheeses twice and asks only whether the cows are alive. For news of them he will write a line under the abbey's seal.
Hunger again, and now the law forbids carrying food out of the realm. Thiadlint has her daughter's price put by, less eleven pennies, and barley is what stands between the eleven and nothing.
Thiadlint stops her loom when a grain boat lands. Rye at the king's price is paid for in cheese; at the strand's price it costs her own bolt.

endings.how: Sold grain here at or under the king's price in a hungry year (the thread's flag hy_fed_poor).
endings.text: Thiadlint weaves for you first from then on, at the price of the place that makes it. In time her daughter is free, and married on the strand, and names a son for your house.
endings.reward: Frisian cloth here at source price for this house, before Radward sees it; standing in the district; the priest names you at the cross; a friend in the next generation.

endings.how: Sold at the strand's price while people were eating seed corn (the thread's flag hy_sold_dear).
endings.text: The silver is good. Folcrad notches the sale and sends the stick up river with the rest. Thiadlint sells you cloth at forty-eight pennies, exactly, for the rest of her life.
endings.reward: A quick profit; the count's men may ask about it at Dorestad; no source price here; Bernrad says your name at the cross in a different voice.

endings.how: Carried the farm's cloth and cheeses to Ghent for nothing and brought back the cellarer's line.
endings.text: The abbey has its due and a merchant it knows by name. The line under its seal makes you Saint Peter's carrier for Witle, a small thing that toll men read slowly and respect.
endings.reward: Welcome and lodging at Ganda; a yearly carrying commission between Witla and Ganda; the farm's surplus cheese and butter offered to you first.

stories.reward: Cloth at source and a family that knows your house, or silver and a notch on the wrong stick, or an abbey's name beside yours.

stories.title: The last seasons
stories.summary: From 834 the fleets pass this mouth every summer on their way to Dorestad, and the strand lives with its boats half loaded and its silver in the ground. In 836 the Northmen burn Witla and Antwerp and take tribute from the Frisians; the market is not rebuilt, and the pilot's family take their marks elsewhere.
stories.picture: Night at the river mouth: a fire burning in the basket on the mark, the ridge of roofs black against it, small boats being pushed off the mud by people wading, and far out on the dark water a line of low hulls with shields along them, coming in on the flood.

beats.text: Gerbrand has counted keels going up by night, and they did not ask for a pilot. He asks whether you are for Dorestad, and whether they would listen there to a merchant who had seen it.

Count Eggihard is over from the island, counting spears. He wants a fire on the mark when sails are seen and wants to know from every skipper how many and how far. The pilot says the fire will show them the houses.

Half the hurdles are empty. Cloth is cheap because nobody will hold it; wine is dear because nobody will bring it. People who can are moving stores inland by the creeks and asking who has a boat free.
Word carried from the Maas mouth that a fleet has passed is worth a day there, if it is believed: time to get silver in the ground and boats up river (the thread's flag df_warned).

This year the Northmen burned Witla. Those who had boats ready went up the creeks; the houses, the racks and the king's post burned, and the tribute was paid in what was left. Gerbrand stands on the bank with the pole and nowhere to pilot anyone to.
The fort on the Scheldt burned the same summer. Men from both places sleep in the same boat sheds and compare what they saved.
On the seventeenth day of June the island falls and the count is killed. Anyone who went there from Witla for safety chose badly.

endings.how: Took the pilot on after the burning.
endings.text: Gerbrand comes aboard with the pole and a bag. He knows the Maas mouth, the creeks through to the Scheldt and the Thames to the Strand, and he sounds everything twice. His children grow up in your home port.
endings.reward: A pilot in the crew for the rest of his life (in the engine's words: hire pilot), and after him his son; the Maas mouth and the Scheldt creeks safe for this house when they are not for others.

endings.how: Gave him bread and silver to set up on the far shore, by the church.
endings.text: The family cross to the north bank and keep the marks there. Six lifetimes on, when a count builds a fort at Vlaardingen and takes his toll, the man who brings the Tiel ships in to pay it has a pole with old notches under the new.
endings.reward: No pilot now, but a friend at the river mouth in every later age: news and a safe crossing there after 836, and in 1018 a warning about the count's toll before your heir reaches it.

endings.how: Carried the family to Walichrum, where there was a count and a wall of men.
endings.text: It was the sensible choice for one winter. In June the island falls. Whether any of them were among those carried off, the survivors disagree, and Sliesthorp is where such things are learned.
endings.reward: A debt of conscience and a thread to follow: word of them may be had among the captives sold in the north, for a price.

endings.how: Carried Gerbrand's count of keels up river in time, and moved your own stores.
endings.text: Dorestad has a day it would not have had. Your stores lie safe inland, and you sell from them to the burned-out at a fair price, which is remembered longer than a high one.
endings.reward: Standing at Dorestad and Witla both; your own goods saved; the count's thanks while he lives, which is one more year.

stories.reward: The last pilot of Witla, in your boat or in your debt; and the knowledge of who was warned in time.

works.name: A corner of the net shed
works.what: Room under the pilot's roof for a few casks and bolts between crossings, with Wilsuit's eye on it. Goods wait here for a wind without paying the strand's price twice.
works.needs: Gerlef or Gerbrand at least easy with you.
works.gives: Store up to a boatload at Witla; nothing stored here is safe in 836 unless it was moved inland first.
works.picture: The inside of a turf shed: nets overhead, three casks and a stack of cloth bolts in a dry corner, a tally stick stuck in the wall above them.
works.source: works_793.json store_corner; the shed is ours

works.name: A fire on the mark
works.what: A better post on the dune mound, an iron basket, and furze and peat paid for a season, so that the mark can be found at dusk and in haze. The pilot chooses the nights.
works.needs: Known in the port; the pilot's good will, since he must keep it.
works.gives: Coming in at dusk or in haze is no longer doubtful at the Maas mouth, for you and for everyone; standing with skippers of this coast. In 834-836 the same fire is an argument: the count wants it lit and the pilot does not.
works.picture: A turf mound at the end of the ridge at dusk, a tall post with an iron basket of fire on it, sparks blowing seaward, one small boat coming in on the line of it.
works.source: works_793.json beacon: in 811 Charles had the old lighthouse at Boulogne put right and a fire lit on it at night (Royal Frankish Annals 811). A mark at Witla is ours

works.name: Sheep on the salt marsh
works.what: Forty ewes run with the strand's flocks on the marsh, shorn before Saint John's day; the wool goes to the looms here and the cloth comes back to you by Lammas.
works.needs: A herdsman's word for you; no flood in the bargain: a storm tide drowns sheep and there are no dykes.
works.gives: A few bolts of Frisian cloth each Lammas at no price but the weaving; lost in a flood year or a murrain, and in 836.
works.picture: Grey sheep scattered over a wide green marsh cut by silver creeks, a boy with a long leaping pole among them, the ridge of roofs small on the skyline.
works.source: works_793.json flock_share; the sheep pasture given with the Maas-mouth church in 726/727, and a coast rich in sheep (Dijkstra 2011, pp. 282, 308-315)

works.name: A pan with the salt burners
works.what: A clay pan, a cutting of salt peat and a share of the ash mound out on the marsh, worked by the burners for a third. Peat salt is grey and bitter and sells wherever fish is cured.
works.needs: Leave of the toll man, since the marsh is the king's (?); a boat to bring the sacks off.
works.gives: Sacks of salt each summer at source; fish cured on the racks with your own salt keeps longer and sells further.
works.picture: A flat brown marsh under low smoke: a black peat cutting, grey ash heaps, a wide clay pan steaming over embers, two ash-coloured figures raking.
works.source: works_793.json salt_pan (Godebert's seventeen salt 'kitchens' in Zeeland, given to Lorsch in 776); only the islands in the Maas mouth were fit for salt in South Holland (Dijkstra 2011, pp. 308-315)

works.name: A bell for the cross
works.what: A small hand bell of riveted iron dipped in bronze, such as the missionaries carried, and a thatched roof on four posts over the cross and the priest's stone. Bernrad has priced both.
works.needs: Bernrad friendly; the bell bought where bells are made, up the Rhine or over the water, and carried here.
works.gives: Mass at Witla is heard by the whole strand; your house is prayed for by name at the cross; standing with the church on both banks. The bell goes over the water with the priest in 836 and is rung on the north bank after.
works.picture: The tall wooden cross on the ridge under a new thatched roof on four posts, a thin tonsured priest ringing a small four-sided hand bell, people coming up from the boats.
works.source: invented in the period's manner: riveted iron hand bells of the Irish and English missions (the bell called Saint Patrick's; Willibrord's own mission came from Ireland) (?); works_793.json bell is the larger cast kind

ships.note: The strand's own boats are of this size: four men, a sail, light enough to drag above the tide line. One is for sale most autumns, when a skipper has had enough.
ships.picture: A small clinker boat on rollers above the tide line, her mast down and lashed, a man walking round her knocking on the strakes.
ships.source: ship_classes_793.json gislinge (a later Danish find standing in: nobody names the Frisian small boat's type); no ship is found at the Maas mouth (dossier 4)

ships.note: River freighters on a log keel come down the Maas with wine and stone and are sold here by men who would rather walk home than haul her back against the stream.
ships.picture: A long round-bottomed river freighter lying on the creek mud, empty, a hauling rope coiled on her bow, her crew arguing a price with a man on the bank.
ships.source: ship_classes_793.json logboat_expanded (the forerunner of the Utrecht ship); peoples/frisian.md 6

ships.note: Flat little creek boats for the nets and the crossing to the north bank; the priest rows one. Useful as a lighter when she must lie off.
ships.picture: A flat punt with one oar and a wet net in her, pulled up among the reeds of a creek.

ships.how: built to order over a winter
ships.note: The round-hulled trader that crosses to Lundenwic. A wright will set one up on the creek bank for a man the strand knows, with oak brought down the Maas and paid for in advance; she is ready at Easter.
ships.picture: A half-planked round hull on stocks on the creek bank in winter, frost on the timber, a wright with an adze, oak logs lying in the mud where the river boat left them.
ships.source: ship_classes_793.json north_sea_merchant_ship; story/unlocks_793.json unlock_ship_north_sea_merchant_ship names Witla among the places she can be ordered; oak from the Ardennes by the Maas is Design/content/ships.md (later centuries; for 793 a guess (?))

sayings.text: Dear is the welcome guest to the Frisian wife, when the vessel stands.
sayings.source: Exeter Book, Gnomic Verses (Thorpe 1842), as given in Design/content/peoples/frisian.md 8

sayings.text: What is the good of those little napkins? I cannot cover myself with them in bed.
sayings.source: King Charles on the short cloaks the Frisians sold at the long price: Notker, Gesta Karoli I.34 (Grant 1907), as given in peoples/frisian.md 8. Said on this strand with some pride.

sayings.text: Frisian robes: white, grey, red and blue.
sayings.source: Notker II.9 (Grant 1907): the cloth the emperor sent as gifts; what the market hurdles show

sayings.text: I will swear alone. You, if you dare, deny my oath and fight me.
sayings.source: Lex Frisionum XI.3, our rendering as in peoples/frisian.md 9; what a man says at the toll post when he has no kin with him

sayings.text: Pull a man out of the water and you are owed four shillings. Nobody on this strand has ever asked for them.
sayings.source: the first sentence is Lex Frisionum XXII.87 (peoples/frisian.md 12); the second is invented in the period's manner
Alcuin's word for the bishop of Utrecht, vaccipotens, in the poem he sent down the Rhine (Carmina IV; Dijkstra 2011, p. 279), paraphrased. The priest repeats it when the tithe men come.

sayings.text: The bar has no friends. It only has people it has not met yet.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner: the pilot's

sayings.text: The first boat sells dear, the second sells, the third carries it home again.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner: a skipper's proverb for a place where news is the cargo

sayings.text: The tide is the only bell we have, and it rings twice.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner; the double low water at this mouth is a modern figure carried back (Research/water_levels/north_sea_core.md) (?)

sayings.text: This year the Northmen burned Witla. That is all that was written of us, and it was written by a man who never came.
sayings.source: invented, turning the one sentence of the Annales Fuldenses 836; said after the burning

easter_eggs.text: At a very low spring ebb, heavy squared stones break the water off the south head, like the footings of a wall. The pilot has put his pole on them and has no name for who built it.
easter_eggs.source: At a very low tide in 1752 Jan Kluit of Brielle saw such stones off Oostvoorne, probably Roman, perhaps a fort (Dijkstra 2011, p. 454). The game shows them a thousand years early, as old then as now

easter_eggs.text: In the toll man's scale pan lies a small thick old penny with a bearded face on one side and a beast on the other, and a little gold piece with the name MADELINVS on it. He weighs with them and will not sell them: nobody strikes such things now.
easter_eggs.source: Dredged from the river mouth in 1959-1976, washed out of place: a penny of the 'Wodan and monster' kind and a gold tremissis of the Dorestad moneyer Madelinus, with five pennies of Louis the Pious. Dijkstra lists them as 'settlement and/or grave field', not as Witla (2011, pp. 266, 451-452)

easter_eggs.text: Count the cows on Saint Peter's farm: there are five, and four people work it. There were five and four when the farm was given, and there will be five and four in the abbey's book long after the sea has the pasture.
easter_eggs.source: The gift of Rathadus: grazing for five cows and four serfs, in a note copied at Ghent in 941, a century after Witla burned (Dijkstra 2011, p. 175; Gysseling 1960)

easter_eggs.text: In a creek on the north shore somebody has left a whole grey spouted pot standing in the mud beside butchered cattle and sheep bone, and not come back for it. The priest will not say what it is. Wilsuit says it is a pot.
easter_eggs.source: A whole Badorf spouted pot left in a creek at Maassluis with butchered cattle and sheep bone (Dijkstra 2011, p. 451). That it was an offering is nobody's claim but the game's hint (?)

easter_eggs.text: Ask the priest the name of the place in the fen behind his church. He gives it at last: Harg. In the old speech it means a heathen altar, and it is still the name on the abbey's own list of what the church owns.
easter_eggs.source: Harago, later Kethel, behind Vlaardingen: the name means 'heathen shrine'; Dijkstra thinks Willibrord may have wanted the church set against it (2011, pp. 288, 301)

easter_eggs.text: After 836 a ship that anchors off the old creek at slack water brings up, once, a net with a bronze pin in it, a spearhead and a piece of a glass cup.
easter_eggs.source: Dredged at west Rozenburg when the harbours were dug: bronze pins, brooches, four spearheads, a piece of a glass tumbler, Carolingian sherds, human bone (Dijkstra 2011, pp. 451-452)

easter_eggs.text: Wilsuit's well is a wine cask with the ends knocked out, sunk in the ridge. On one stave a cooper up the Rhine has cut a mark like a bird's foot. Every well on this coast is somebody's empty wine.
easter_eggs.source: Old Rhenish wine casks line wells in every settlement of this coast (Dijkstra 2011, pp. 308-315); the cooper's mark is ours

unlocks.what: The marks of the Maas bar and of the Thames to the Strand, by heart
unlocks.how: End 'Paid by the year' as the pilot's pupil: come back over several seasons, ask Gerlef about the water, bring the boy a lead line from Lundenwic.
unlocks.gives: learn (the Maas-mouth and Thames marks): no pilot is needed and nothing is doubtful at this bar or below Lundenwic for this house; inherited.

unlocks.what: The pilot's family as friends of the house, for as long as there is a family
